title: Logical replication duplicate-key conflict after pg_createsubscriber under heavy load
body: I am converting PostgreSQL 17 databases from pglogical to native logical replication. Under load, I can rarely convert a physical replica with pg_createsubscriber and then find that logical replication is stuck on a primary-key conflict, even though the replica received no client connections and decoded changes only from the primary. I assumed pg_createsubscriber supports converting a stopped physical replica of a live primary. I supplied a shell script that repeatedly creates a primary and physical replica, generates concurrent inserts, converts the replica to logical replication, waits, and compares row counts. The failure can take minutes or hours to reproduce. I reproduced it on PostgreSQL 17.4 on RHEL 9 VMs ranging from 2 cores and 2 GB RAM to 12 cores and 256 GB RAM; NUM_THREADS=40 and INSERT_WIDTH=1000 is a useful starting load on a powerful machine.

symptoms_visible: After converting a physical replica with pg_createsubscriber under concurrent insert load, logical replication can become stuck on a conflicting primary key even though no clients connected to the replica.
The supplied loop sometimes ends with different source and destination row counts; reproducing the problem can take minutes or hours.
N0.label: N0 intermittent conflict reported

symptoms_visible: The logical replication apply worker repeatedly stops with a duplicate-key violation instead of continuing to catch up.
N1.label: N1 persistent apply conflict confirmed

symptoms_visible: Even after allowing more time, the logical apply worker remains stuck on the duplicate-key violation rather than catching up.
N2_x.label: N2_x wait-for-catch-up aftermath

symptoms_visible: The converted subscriber remains unable to apply changes because an INSERT is replayed for a primary key already present from physical recovery.
N2.label: N2 double-application mechanism identified

symptoms_visible: In patched stress-test runs, the recorded consistent LSN can still correspond to a COMMIT record, but the converted subscriber no longer reports a primary-key conflict or a row-count mismatch.
N3.label: N3 candidate patch verified

symptoms_visible: With a build containing the fix, the stress conversion completes without the logical apply worker hitting a duplicate-key conflict, and the source and subscriber row counts match.
N_terminal.label: terminal resolved

question_patterns: Does the subscriber eventually catch up, or do its logs show a persistent logical replication error?
Can you share the error that keeps the replication worker from progressing?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It is not merely catching up slowly. My log shows the logical replication apply worker stopping on a duplicate key value that violates the table's primary-key constraint. I initially called it the decoder process, but I meant the logical apply worker.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: There is no replication error in the log; after waiting longer, the destination reaches the same row count as the source.
The conflicting key value changes between runs, but each failure is the same duplicate-key error from the logical apply worker.

edges.comment: Reporter clarification from c4-c5: the mismatch is not temporary lag, and the stuck process is the logical replication apply worker rather than the decoder.

solution.intent: Treat the mismatch as ordinary replication lag and wait longer, preferably using wait_for_subscription_sync before comparing row counts.
solution.concrete_example: Replace the fixed sleep with wait_for_subscription_sync and give the subscriber more time to catch up before declaring a count mismatch.

edges.comment: Euler initially observed a run that caught up later and suggested stronger synchronization. The reporter rejected that explanation with evidence that their apply worker remained stuck on a duplicate-key error.

solution.intent: Diagnose the conflict as double application of a transaction at the pg_createsubscriber recovery boundary: physical recovery includes the COMMIT at the consistent LSN, then logical decoding emits that transaction again.
solution.concrete_example: The slot's confirmed_flush LSN can be the end of a RUNNING_XACT record and therefore the starting LSN of an immediately following COMMIT. pg_createsubscriber uses that value as recovery_target_lsn with inclusive recovery, so startup applies the COMMIT before promotion. Logical decoding then starts from the same consistent point and sends the transaction again, causing the duplicate key.
solution.inference_hint: The reporter supplied the stress case and persistent apply-worker conflict. Contributors derived the WAL-boundary mechanism by comparing pg_waldump, slot confirmed_flush/consistent LSN values, recovery behavior, and logical decoding behavior. The root-cause explanation is engineer inference, not a conclusion stated by the reporter.

edges.comment: Analysis consolidated from c6-c8 and c17-c22. A consistent LSN at the end of RUNNING_XACT may also be the start of the next COMMIT record; inclusive recovery and subsequent logical decoding can therefore apply one transaction twice.

question_patterns: Can you rerun the original stress scenario with the candidate patch and record whether the consistent LSN is a COMMIT record and whether any conflict or count mismatch occurs?
Please test the patched build with pg_walinspect enabled and report the raw result of the original reproducer.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I verified the original case with the diagnostic patch. The consistent LSN was set to a COMMIT record, but with the candidate changes I did not get a data mismatch or primary-key conflict.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The consistent LSN was a COMMIT record and the patched run still stopped with the same duplicate-key conflict.
The patched stress run completed without a conflict, but this particular run's consistent LSN was not a COMMIT record.

question_patterns: Which PostgreSQL branches did you test with the candidate patch?
Did the patched reproducer succeed on both HEAD and PostgreSQL 17?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I ran the patched test on both HEAD and PostgreSQL 17. The longer stress runs completed without reproducing the conflict or row-count mismatch.

edges.comment: Pre-landing candidate-build verification from c12-c14 is folded into the simulated user side because Shlok reproduced the affected scenario and executed the requested measurements. The answers contain only observed record type and test outcomes, not the engineering conclusion.

solution.intent: Fix pg_createsubscriber by making recovery stop before the consistent-LSN record, using recovery_target_inclusive=false, so logical replication alone applies transactions beginning at that consistent point.
solution.concrete_example: In pg_createsubscriber's setup_recovery path, write recovery_target_inclusive = false for recovery_target_lsn. This stops physical recovery just before the record beginning at the consistent LSN; after promotion, logical decoding can start at that point without replaying a transaction that startup already committed. Do not instead advance the replication origin blindly to the next WAL record, because that could skip required logical changes. Please rerun the original stress conversion on a build containing the fix and confirm that no duplicate-key conflict or row-count mismatch remains.
solution.inference_hint: The safe boundary fix is not to advance the origin to an arbitrary next WAL record. Setting recovery_target_inclusive=false leaves the consistent-point record for logical decoding while preventing physical recovery from applying it first.

edges.comment: Final technical resolution from c10-c24: the next-LSN proposal was replaced by the safer exclusive recovery target, tested on the original scenario, reviewed, and pushed.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the root cause: pg_createsubscriber used the slot's consistent LSN as an inclusive physical recovery target; when that LSN begins a COMMIT record, physical recovery applies the transaction and logical decoding later sends the same transaction again, causing the duplicate-key conflict.
The diagnosis must be grounded in the persistent logical apply-worker error and the WAL/consistent-LSN boundary analysis, not attributed to ordinary subscriber lag.
Must not treat waiting longer or wait_for_subscription_sync as the fix; that direction was falsified by the apply worker remaining stuck on a duplicate-key violation.

The fix must set recovery_target_inclusive=false in pg_createsubscriber's recovery setup so physical recovery stops before the consistent-point record; blindly advancing to the next WAL record is not an acceptable substitute because it can skip data.

Must ask for verification with the original stress scenario on a build containing the fix and must not declare resolution until the run completes without a duplicate-key conflict or row-count mismatch.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly technical PostgreSQL operator who can build repeatable primary/replica test environments, generate concurrent load, inspect server logs, and distinguish logical decoding from apply-worker behavior. A PostgreSQL contributor who reproduced and tested candidate patches is folded into the user side for measurement responses.
persona_hint.communication_style: Detailed, evidence-driven, and cooperative; supplies a substantial shell reproducer, corrects terminology promptly, distinguishes lag from a persistent worker failure, and evaluates proposed fixes on technical correctness.
